answers.text: Use a fixed three-line template — drop-off time, pallet count, damage — always in that order. Each line gets a precise definition, so there's no ambiguity about what goes where. If any field is missing, say to write 'not stated', never leave it blank or invent a figure.

Specify the list structure exactly: one line per call, fixed fields, a follow-up flag on each. State that the follow-up count is derived by summing the flagged entries, not asserted separately. Say explicitly what to do with a duplicate-looking entry — flag it, don't silently merge or drop it.
There's an internal inconsistency in how the visit's timing is described. The six-hour estimate from an 8am start resolves same-day, so the note's finish date doesn't follow.

Recalculating, 96 to 118 comes out at about 23%, not the stated 20%. The on-time rate itself is consistent: 9 late out of 118 is roughly 92%, matching what's stated. The steady balance figure sits oddly against a >20% invoice rise the same month, unaddressed.

Output 2 is the one to approve, since the number is derived, not asserted. Output 1 leaves out the two figures behind the percentage — total tickets and SLA closures. Output 1's figure isn't necessarily wrong, only unconfirmable without an independent re-count.

I'd send Email 2 without further checking — it cites the volume figures and PO log. The claim in Email 1 that can't be checked is the rate expectation itself; nothing supports it. I wouldn't reject Email 1 outright; add the PO log figures and it becomes equally sendable.

The rate figures get redacted or held back until the tool itself is vetted. The non-disclosure clause names both parties directly, its own reason for caution beyond the rates. The service scope itself is low-risk and fine to paste as-is — no need to redact plain description.
I'd add a named cross-cast step: recompute the month's stock totals independently and compare. That check sits right before the reconciliation reaches finance, not earlier in the process.

Step 1 — extracting line items and totals — carries risk that compounds through every step after. Step 4 is where an error becomes irreversible — once it auto-submits, there's no catching it after. Concretely: flag an extracted total above a threshold, or a match level at the tolerance cutoff, for review.
